p.src: Now, in the first month of the second year of Zhengyuan in Wei, Guanqiu Jian, courtesy name Zhonggong, a native of Wenxi in Henan, was Inspector of Yangzhou and General Who Guards the East, commanding the troops of Huainan. When he heard that Sima Shi had arbitrarily deposed one sovereign and installed another, he was filled with indignation. His eldest son, Guanqiu Dian, said, “Father, you hold command over an entire region. Sima Shi has seized power and deposed the sovereign, placing the state in peril like eggs piled one upon another. How can you remain at ease and merely guard your own position?” Jian replied, “What you say is right, my son.” He therefore invited Inspector Wen Qin to confer with him. Wen Qin had formerly been a retainer of Cao Shuang. On hearing that Jian wished to see him, he came at once to pay his respects. Jian invited him into the rear hall, and after they had exchanged the proper courtesies, as they talked, Jian began to weep without cease. Wen Qin asked him why. Jian said, “Sima Shi has usurped authority and deposed the sovereign, overturning the order of Heaven and Earth. How could I not grieve?” Wen Qin said, “You command and guard this region. If you are willing to uphold righteousness and punish the traitor, I am willing to risk my life in your aid. My second son, Wen Shu, whose childhood name is A-Yang, possesses courage that ten thousand men could not withstand. He has long wished to kill Sima Shi and his brother to avenge Cao Shuang. He may now be appointed vanguard.” Jian was overjoyed and at once poured a libation of wine and swore an oath. The two men falsely proclaimed that the Empress Dowager had issued a secret edict. They ordered every civil and military officer and soldier in Huainan to enter Shouchun, erected an altar in the west, slaughtered a white horse, and smeared its blood upon their lips in covenant. They declared that Sima Shi had committed monstrous treason and that, acting upon the Empress Dowager’s secret edict, they were mustering all the forces of Huainan to uphold righteousness and punish the traitor. All were pleased and submitted to their command. Jian led sixty thousand troops and encamped at Xiangcheng. Wen Qin commanded twenty thousand troops as a mobile force outside the city, moving to and fro to provide support. Jian circulated a proclamation among the commanderies, ordering each of them to raise troops and come to his aid.

p.src: Now Sima Shi had a tumor on his left eye that frequently caused pain and itching. He ordered a court physician to cut it away and seal the wound with medicine, and for several days he remained at his residence recuperating. Suddenly hearing that Huainan was in crisis, he summoned Grand Commandant Wang Su to consult with him. Wang Su said, “Formerly, when Guan Yunchang’s might shook all the lands of China, Sun Quan ordered Lü Meng to seize Jingzhou by surprise and showed generous care to the families of Guan’s officers and men. As a result, Lord Guan’s army collapsed. The families of the Huainan officers and men are now all in the Central Plains. If you promptly treat them with generosity and then use troops to cut off the rebels’ route home, their forces will surely crumble.” Sima Shi said, “Your words are entirely right. But I have only just had the tumor cut from my eye and cannot go in person; yet if I send another, my mind will not be at ease.” At that time, Zhong Hui, Gentleman Attendant of the Palace Secretariat, stood nearby and advised, “The troops of Huainan and Chu are strong, and their onset is exceedingly fierce. If another man is sent to lead the army against them, the outcome will most likely be unfavorable. Should any mishap occur, the great enterprise will be ruined.” Sima Shi sprang to his feet and declared, “Unless I go myself, the rebels cannot be defeated!” He therefore left his younger brother Sima Zhao to guard Luoyang and assume overall charge of the court government. Sima Shi rode in a padded litter and journeyed east despite his illness. He ordered Zhuge Dan, General Who Guards the East, to take overall command of the armies of Yuzhou and advance from Anfeng Ford to seize Shouchun. He also ordered Hu Zun, General Who Conquers the East, to lead the armies of Qingzhou through the region of Qiao and Song and cut off the rebels’ road home. He further dispatched Wang Ji, Inspector of Yuzhou and Army Supervisor, to lead the vanguard and first seize the territory of Zhennan. Sima Shi led the main army to encamp at Xiangyang and assembled the civil and military officers beneath his command tent to deliberate.

p.src: Zheng Bao, Minister of the Imperial Household, said, “Guanqiu Jian is fond of schemes but lacks decisiveness, while Wen Qin has courage but no wisdom. Our great army has now taken them by surprise. Yet the soldiers of the Yangzi and Huai regions are at the height of their ardor and must not be underestimated. We should do no more than dig deep moats and raise high ramparts to blunt their spirit. This is the master strategy once used by Zhou Yafu.” Army Supervisor Wang Ji said, “No. This revolt in Huainan did not arise because the soldiers and common people desired disorder. They have all been compelled by Guanqiu Jian’s power and had no choice but to follow him. Once our great army arrives, they will surely fall apart.” Sima Shi said, “That is excellent counsel.” He then advanced to the banks of the Yin River, stationing his central army at Yin Bridge. Wang Ji said, “Nandun is an excellent place to station troops. We should march through the night and seize it. If we delay, Guanqiu Jian will surely arrive first.” Sima Shi accordingly ordered Wang Ji to lead the vanguard to Nandun and establish a camp beneath its walls.

p.src: Now Guanqiu Jian was at Xiangcheng. When he learned that Sima Shi had come in person, he assembled his officers to deliberate. The vanguard commander Ge Yong said, “Nandun lies beside mountains and water and is an excellent place to station troops. If the Wei army occupies it first, it will be difficult to dislodge them. We must seize it quickly.” Jian followed his advice, raised his army, and marched toward Nandun. While they were on the march, a courier on a fleet horse reported from the front that troops had already established a camp at Nandun. Jian did not believe it and went forward himself to inspect. Sure enough, banners covered the fields and the encampment stood in perfect order. Jian returned to his army, at a loss for any plan. Suddenly a scout galloped in with the report: “Sun Jun of Eastern Wu has led troops across the river and is coming to raid Shouchun!” Jian cried in alarm, “If Shouchun is lost, where shall I return to?” That night he withdrew his army to Xiangcheng. When Sima Shi saw Guanqiu Jian’s army retreat, he assembled his officers to confer. Fu Jia, Master of Writing, said, “Jian has retreated because he fears the men of Wu will raid Shouchun. He will surely return to Xiangcheng and divide his forces for its defense. General, you should order one army to seize Lejia, another to seize Xiangcheng, and a third to seize Shouchun. Then the troops of Huainan will surely withdraw. Deng Ai, Inspector of Yanzhou, is resourceful and full of stratagems. If he leads troops directly against Lejia and you support him with a powerful army, defeating the rebels will not be difficult.” Sima Shi accepted his advice and urgently dispatched a messenger with a written command, ordering Deng Ai to raise the troops of Yanzhou and seize Lejia. Sima Shi would then lead his army there to join him.

p.src: Now Guanqiu Jian, at Xiangcheng, repeatedly sent men to scout Lejia, fearing that an enemy force might come. He summoned Wen Qin to the camp for consultation, and Wen Qin said, “Commander, do not worry. My unworthy son Wen Yang and I need only five thousand troops, and I guarantee that we shall hold Lejia.” Jian was delighted. Wen Qin and his son led five thousand troops toward Lejia. The vanguard reported, “To the west of Lejia there are Wei troops everywhere, numbering more than ten thousand. Looking toward the central army from afar, we saw white yak-tail standards and yellow battle-axes, black canopies and vermilion banners, clustered around the commander’s tiger tent. Within it stands a brocade commander’s banner bearing the character ‘Marshal.’ This must be Sima Shi. They are setting up camp, but their defenses are not yet complete.” At that moment Wen Yang stood beside his father with his whip hanging at his side. Hearing the report, he said to him, “While their camp is still unfinished, we can divide our troops into two columns and strike from left and right. We shall win a complete victory.” Wen Qin asked, “When should we set out?” Wen Yang replied, “At dusk tonight, Father, lead two thousand five hundred troops and attack from the south of the city. I shall lead two thousand five hundred troops and attack from the north. At the third watch, we must meet within the Wei camp.” Wen Qin agreed, and that evening they divided their troops into two columns. Now Wen Yang was only eighteen years old. He stood eight chi tall, fully armed and clad in armor, with a steel whip at his waist. Seizing his spear, he mounted his horse and advanced toward the distant Wei camp.

p.src: That night, Sima Shi's army reached Lejia, pitched camp, and waited for Deng Ai, who had not yet arrived. Sima Shi had recently had a growth cut from beneath his eye, and the wound was painfully inflamed. He lay in his tent with several hundred armored guards standing all around him. At the third watch, a sudden roar of battle shook the camp, and men and horses were thrown into chaos. Sima Shi urgently asked what had happened. A man reported, “A force has broken through the northern enclosure and charged straight in. The general at its head is irresistibly brave.” Sima Shi was greatly alarmed; his heart blazed like fire, and his eyeball burst out through the wound where the growth had been removed. Blood streamed over the ground, and the pain was unbearable; yet fearing that an outcry might shake the army's morale, he merely bit down on his quilt and endured it, tearing the quilt to shreds with his teeth. It turned out that Wen Yang's troops had arrived first and surged into the camp together; they charged left and right throughout the camp, and none dared oppose them wherever they went; any who resisted were stabbed with the spear or struck with the whip, and not one escaped death. Wen Yang looked only for his father's arrival, expecting support from outside, but there was no sign of him. Several times he fought his way to the central command, but each time volleys of bows and crossbows drove him back. Wen Yang fought straight through until dawn, when he heard drums and horns resounding to the heavens in the north. He looked back at his followers and said, “Why has my father come from the north instead of supporting me from the south?” Wen Yang spurred forward to look and saw an army advancing like a fierce gale. Its leading general was Deng Ai, who brandished his saber on horseback and cried, “Rebel, do not flee!” Wen Yang flew into a rage and leveled his spear to meet him. They fought fifty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. While they were locked in combat, the Wei troops surged forward and attacked from front and rear. Wen Yang's soldiers scattered and fled, leaving him alone on a single horse. He broke through the Wei troops and fled south. Behind him, several hundred Wei officers summoned their strength and galloped in pursuit; as they neared Lejia Bridge, they were on the point of overtaking him. Suddenly Wen Yang reined his horse around, gave a mighty shout, and charged straight into the ranks of the Wei officers, his steel whip rising and falling. They tumbled from their horses one after another, and all the rest fell back. Wen Yang then resumed his unhurried way. The Wei officers gathered together and exclaimed in astonishment, “Does this man still dare drive back so many of us? Let us join forces and pursue him!” And so a hundred Wei officers again gave chase. Wen Yang burst into fury and cried, “You rats, do you value your lives so little?” Whip in hand, he wheeled his horse and charged among the Wei officers, beat several of them to death, then turned again and rode slowly on with loose reins. The Wei officers pursued him four or five times, and every time Wen Yang alone drove them back. A later poet wrote:

Seeing that the Wei army had won a great victory, Wen Qin retreated without fighting. The Wei troops pressed their advantage and pursued, while Wen Qin led his men toward Shouchun.

p.src: Now Yin Damu, Palace Commandant of Wei, had been one of Cao Shuang's trusted men; because Cao Shuang had been murdered through Sima Yi's scheming, Yin Damu served Sima Shi while constantly harboring the desire to kill him and avenge Cao Shuang; moreover, he had long been on close terms with Wen Qin. Now, seeing Sima Shi's eye protruding and that he could neither move nor rise, he entered the tent and said, “Wen Qin originally had no intention of rebelling. He has come to this only because Guanqiu Jian forced him into it. If I go and persuade him, he will certainly come and surrender.” Sima Shi agreed. Damu donned helmet and armor, mounted his horse, and rode after Wen Qin; when he was close to catching him, he shouted, “Inspector Wen, do you see Yin Damu?” Wen Qin looked back. Damu removed his helmet, placed it before the saddle bow, pointed with his whip, and said, “Inspector Wen, why could you not endure for just a few more days?” Damu knew that Sima Shi was about to die and had therefore come to make Wen Qin stay. Wen Qin failed to grasp his meaning, cursed him harshly, and made ready to draw his bow and shoot. Damu wept bitterly and turned back. When Wen Qin gathered his troops and hastened to Shouchun, Zhuge Dan had already led an army there and taken it; when he turned back toward Xiangcheng, the three armies of Hu Zun, Wang Ji, and Deng Ai had all arrived. Seeing the danger of his position, Wen Qin went over to Sun Jun of Eastern Wu.

p.src: Meanwhile, Guanqiu Jian was in Xiangcheng when he learned that Shouchun had fallen, Wen Qin had been defeated, and three armies had arrived outside the city. He therefore withdrew every soldier from the city and led them out to battle. He encountered Deng Ai, and ordered Ge Yong to ride out and engage him. Before a single bout was over, Deng Ai cut Ge Yong down with one stroke of his saber, then led his troops charging through the formation. Guanqiu Jian fought desperately to resist him. The troops from the Jiang and Huai regions fell into great disorder. Hu Zun and Wang Ji led their troops in attacks from every side. Unable to withstand them, Guanqiu Jian took little more than ten riders and forced a path of escape. When he reached the walls of Shen County, the magistrate Song Bai opened the gates to welcome him and laid out a banquet. Guanqiu Jian became thoroughly drunk, whereupon Song Bai ordered his men to kill him and presented his head to the Wei army. Thus Huainan was pacified.

p.src: Sima Shi lay ill and could not rise. He summoned Zhuge Dan into his tent, bestowed seals of office upon him, promoted him to Senior General Who Conquers the East, and placed him in command of all the forces in Yang Province; at the same time, he ordered the army to return to Xuchang. The pain in Sima Shi's eye never ceased, and every night he saw Li Feng, Zhang Ji, and Xiahou Xuan standing before his bed. His mind wandered, and knowing that he was unlikely to survive, he sent someone to Luoyang to fetch Sima Zhao. Sima Zhao wept and bowed below the bed. Sima Shi gave these last instructions: “The authority I now bear is so great that even if I wished to lay it down, I could not. You must succeed me in wielding it. On no account entrust this great enterprise lightly to another, lest you bring ruin upon our entire clan.” When he had finished, he handed over the seals of office, tears streaming down his face. Just as Sima Zhao was about to ask a question, Sima Shi gave a great cry, his eyeball burst out, and he died. It was the second month of the second year of Zhengyuan. Sima Zhao then announced the mourning and submitted a report to Cao Mao, emperor of Wei. Cao Mao sent an envoy bearing an edict to Xuchang, ordering Sima Zhao to remain there temporarily with the army to guard against Eastern Wu. Sima Zhao hesitated, unable to decide. Zhong Hui said, “The Senior General has only just died, and men's hearts are unsettled. p.src: Jiang Wei therefore led fifty thousand troops toward Fuhan. When the army reached the Tao River, the frontier guards reported its arrival to Wang Jing, Inspector of Yongzhou, and Chen Tai, General Who Conquers the West. Wang Jing was the first to march out, bringing seventy thousand cavalry and infantry to meet him. Jiang Wei gave Zhang Yi certain instructions, then likewise explained another plan to Xiahou Ba. The two departed to carry out their orders, while Jiang Wei himself drew up the main army with its back to the Tao River. Wang Jing rode out with several subordinate commanders and demanded, “Wei, Wu, and Shu have already formed a balance of three powers. Why, then, have you invaded our lands time and again?” Jiang Wei replied, “Sima Shi deposed his sovereign without cause. Neighboring states have every reason to call him to account—how much more so an enemy realm?” Wang Jing looked back at his four commanders, Zhang Ming, Hua Yong, Liu Da, and Zhu Fang, and said, “The Shu troops have formed their line with the river at their backs. If defeated, they will drown in it. Jiang Wei is fierce and valiant; you four can engage him. If he shows any sign of retreating, pursue him at once.” The four commanders rode out from left and right to engage Jiang Wei. After exchanging only a few bouts, Jiang Wei wheeled his horse around and fled toward his own camp. Wang Jing drove all his cavalry and infantry forward in pursuit. Jiang Wei led his troops fleeing westward along the Tao River. As they drew near the water, he cried aloud to his officers and men, “The situation is desperate! Why do you not fight with all your might?” All his commanders turned together and fought back with renewed fury, routing the Wei army. Zhang Yi and Xiahou Ba had circled behind the Wei troops. Attacking from two directions, they trapped the enemy in the center of the encirclement. Displaying all his martial prowess, Jiang Wei charged into the Wei ranks and burst through them left and right. The Wei army fell into chaos and trampled itself; more than half were killed, countless men were driven into the Tao River, over ten thousand heads were taken, and corpses lay heaped for several li. Wang Jing gathered a hundred horsemen from his defeated army, fought his way out with all his strength, and fled straight toward the city of Didao. He rushed into the city, shut the gates, and held fast. Having won a complete victory, Jiang Wei rewarded his troops and then prepared to advance against Didao. Zhang Yi remonstrated, “General, your achievement is complete and your fame resounds far and wide. You should stop here. If you advance now and matters go awry, it will be just like adding feet to a finished painting of a snake.” Jiang Wei replied, “That is not so. Even after our former defeat, I still sought to advance and range across the Central Plain. After today’s battle at the Tao River, the men of Wei are terrified. I judge that Didao can be taken as easily as turning the hand. Do not weaken your own resolve.” Zhang Yi remonstrated again and again, but Jiang Wei would not listen. He marshaled his troops and advanced to seize Didao.

p.src: Meanwhile, Chen Tai, the General Who Conquers the West in Yongzhou, was preparing to raise an army and avenge Wang Jing’s defeat when Deng Ai, Inspector of Yanzhou, suddenly arrived with troops. Chen Tai went to receive him, and after the courtesies were completed, Deng Ai said, “By order of the General-in-Chief, I have come expressly to help you defeat the enemy.” Chen Tai asked Deng Ai for his strategy. Deng Ai said, “After his victory at the Tao River, if Jiang Wei were to rally the Qiang tribes, contend eastward for the passes and the Long region, and send proclamations through the four commanderies, it would be a grave danger to our army. But instead of considering such a course, he covets Didao. Its walls are strong and cannot be taken quickly, so he will merely exhaust his troops to no purpose. I shall now array our forces at Xiang Ridge and then advance to strike him. The Shu army will certainly be defeated.” Chen Tai said, “A truly excellent judgment!” He therefore first detached twenty companies of fifty men each, all equipped with banners, drums, horns, beacon fires, and the like. Traveling by night and hiding by day, they went to lie in ambush among the high mountains and deep valleys southeast of Didao. They were to wait until the enemy came, then beat their drums and sound their horns in unison as a signal; at night they were to raise fires and fire cannon to frighten them. When all arrangements were complete, they waited only for the Shu army to arrive. Chen Tai and Deng Ai then each led twenty thousand troops forward in succession.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei surrounded Didao and ordered his troops to attack from all eight directions. After several days of continuous assaults, the city had not fallen; frustrated, he could devise no further plan. At dusk that day, three or five relays of swift horsemen suddenly came reporting, “Two armies are approaching, with large characters clearly written on their banners. One is led by Chen Tai, General Who Conquers the West, and the other by Deng Ai, Inspector of Yanzhou.” Jiang Wei was greatly alarmed and summoned Xiahou Ba to confer. Xiahou Ba said, “As I once told you, General, Deng Ai has possessed a profound understanding of warfare since childhood and is thoroughly versed in geography. Now that he has come at the head of an army, he will prove a formidable adversary.” Jiang Wei said, “His army has come from afar. We must not allow him to gain a foothold, but strike at once.” He left Zhang Yi to continue the siege and ordered Xiahou Ba to lead troops against Chen Tai. Jiang Wei himself led troops to meet Deng Ai. Before he had gone five li, a cannon suddenly boomed in the southeast; drums and horns shook the earth, and flames surged into the sky. Jiang Wei spurred his horse forward to look and saw Wei banners on every side. Greatly alarmed, he cried, “I have fallen into Deng Ai’s trap!” He immediately sent orders for Xiahou Ba and Zhang Yi each to abandon Didao and withdraw. Thus the entire Shu army withdrew to Hanzhong. Jiang Wei personally guarded the rear and heard the unceasing beat of drums behind him. Only when he had withdrawn into Jiange did he learn that the fires and drums at more than twenty places had all been mere decoys. Jiang Wei gathered his troops and withdrew to camp at Zhongdi.
